Subnets

Subnets divide a VPC address range into Availability-Zone-scoped network segments where routing and placement policy become concrete.

Architecture / mental model

VPC CIDR → subnet A (AZ-a) + subnet B (AZ-b) + subnet C (AZ-c)
subnet → route table + NACL + resources

How it works

A subnet is a CIDR range inside a VPC and lives in exactly one Availability Zone. Multi-AZ designs therefore need separate subnets in each AZ used by the architecture.

Public versus private is primarily a routing description. A subnet associated with a route table that sends internet-bound traffic to an Internet Gateway is public; one without that direct route is private.

Subnet sizing is an address-planning decision. AWS reserves addresses inside each subnet, so CIDR size should reflect future workload count, managed-service requirements and scaling rather than today's two test instances.

Hands-on reference

aws ec2 describe-subnets --query 'Subnets[].[SubnetId,CidrBlock,AvailabilityZone,MapPublicIpOnLaunch]' --output table

Verification

For every subnet, identify its CIDR, Availability Zone, route table, NACL and intended tier. Confirm the actual route path matches the public/private label you use in diagrams.

Field note / gotcha

A subnet is not public because its name contains `public`. Routing to an Internet Gateway is the property that gives the subnet a direct internet path.

Security considerations

Separate tiers and environments where that separation helps policy, but remember subnet boundaries do not replace Security Groups, IAM or application authentication.

What I learned

Subnets turn abstract VPC address space into deployable failure and routing zones.
